 Nets’ Mo Wagner has to root against his brother on Friday night. 
 By C.J. Holmes | cholmes@nydailynews.com | New York Daily News PUBLISHED: November 20, 2026 at 4:18 PM EST Moritz Wagner has spent most of his life rooting for his younger brother. On Friday night, he faced the unfamiliar prospect of hoping Franz would miss.
 It was an unusual position for the Nets center, who grew up playing basketball with Franz in Berlin, followed a similar path to the NBA and spent five seasons alongside him in Orlando. They shared locker rooms, practices, flights and even a home. But Friday’s matchup between Brooklyn and Orlando Magic at Barclays Center marked the first time the brothers were scheduled to face each other as opponents in an organized game.
 Moe wasn’t entirely sure how to feel about it.
 “It’s awkward. I’m not going to lie. I don’t really know how to compartmentalize and really deal with it,” he said before the game. “I’ll try to focus on the game plan and see what happens emotionally.”
 Moe and Franz developed through ALBA Berlin’s youth system before both attended Michigan, although their college careers never overlapped. Moe reached the NBA first, becoming a first-round pick in 2018, and Franz followed three years later when Orlando selected him eighth overall.
 By then, Moe had already joined the Magic. For the next five seasons, the brothers shared an experience few NBA players get to enjoy. They lived together, drove to work together and represented Germany together, helping their country win its first FIBA World Cup championship in 2023.
 For Franz, now 25, having his older brother around was about more than convenience.
 “In life, but also in basketball, too, he was always the one person I was looking up to the most,” Franz told the Magic’s official website. “He paved the way for me in a lot of ways. It made it easy for me to kind of follow his footsteps.”
 Their arrangement ended this summer when Moe signed with Brooklyn. The separation made professional sense, but that didn’t make it entirely easy. Franz explained as much in October, explaining that his brother was excited about his opportunity with the Nets even as both struggled with the end of their time together.
 “He was really happy about his deal in Brooklyn,” he said. “I knew it was a great situation for him. I know he loves New York… We’re both a little sad his time here has come to an end… But he’s in a great spot.”
 Moe, meanwhile, had his own reasons for embracing Brooklyn. At Nets Media Day, he described his conversations with general manager Sean Marks and head coach Jordi Fernández as honest and straightforward. He already knew Fernández from international competition, and New York had long held a particular appeal.
 “I think Brooklyn is as close as it gets in the U.S. to Berlin,” Moe said.
 The brothers entered Friday’s game in considerably different roles.
 Franz had become Orlando’s offensive centerpiece, averaging career highs of 24.4 points and 8.5 assists to go with 6.9 rebounds through 14 games. He’d been even more productive over his previous six appearances, averaging 30.7 points, 7.7 rebounds and 8.5 assists, including four performances with at least 30 points.
 Moe had provided scoring off Brooklyn’s bench, averaging 10.4 points and 3.4 rebounds in 17.9 minutes. Through 14 games, he was shooting 60.7% from the field and an NBA-leading 63% from 3-point range, though the latter figure came on just 27 attempts.
 Brooklyn had struggled defensively during Moe’s minutes, particularly with protecting the rim and rebounding. His playing time had fluctuated, dropping to a season-low 10 minutes against the Philadelphia 76ers on Monday before climbing back to 20 in Wednesday’s loss to the Chicago Bulls.
 Fernández, however, had resisted judging Wagner solely by the Nets’ early lineup numbers.
 “I think [Moe] brings a lot of positives. I know that we all talk about NET rating in 12 games. For whatever it’s worth, I don’t know how big that is,” Fernández said. “Moe brings energy and communication. Obviously, he scores at a high level. And he’s willing to be coached hard and get better. So, I have no concerns with him on the court.”
 Moe is an emotional player who talks constantly, battles for position and takes considerable pleasure in irritating opponents. Franz knows those habits better than just about anyone. He watched them from the same bench for years.
 Friday presented the possibility of experiencing them from the other side.
 The younger Wagner approached the occasion with considerably less apprehension than his brother, describing the matchup as an opportunity their family could appreciate regardless of the outcome.
 “It’s definitely going to be a little weird,” Franz said beforehand. “We’ve obviously played in practice against each other. But I look at it as a huge blessing to be able to share the court together at this level.”
 For Moe, the emotions were harder to untangle. Brooklyn reminded him of Berlin, where he and Franz grew up. But on Friday, the brother who once rode beside him to games was across the court, wearing the other team’s jersey.
